opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think that's the thing I'm most excited about, and it's also the hardest one to measure cleanly. For a long time the way we tracked progress was benchmarks: can the model answer this exam question, can it solve this competition math problem. And those got saturated faster than almost anyone expected. But doing science on your own is a different shape of task. It's not answering a question someone else posed. It's figuring out which question is worth asking, designing the experiment, running it, noticing when the result is weird, and deciding what to do next, over days or weeks instead of seconds.

So the way I think about it now is time horizon and autonomy. How long can a system work productively on a hard, open-ended problem before it needs a human to step in and redirect it? A couple of years ago that was minutes. Now it's meaningfully longer, and you're starting to hear from scientists, mathematicians, biologists, people working on materials, saying, "this thing actually helped me find something I wouldn't have found as fast, or maybe at all." That's a different kind of signal than a benchmark score, and to me it's the more important one.

I'd put us at the stage where AI is a genuinely useful collaborator for a lot of researchers, and occasionally it's contributing something that feels like a real novel insight. Small ones, mostly. But the first time you see that, it changes your intuition about where this goes. The step after that, where a system can run a meaningful chunk of a research program with a human mostly setting direction and checking the work, I think that's coming sooner than people assume, though I've learned to be humble about exact timelines.

And the reason I care so much about it: if you ask what actually makes people's lives better over the long run, a huge part of the answer is scientific progress. Curing diseases, cheaper energy, better materials. If AI can meaningfully speed up the rate of discovery, that's probably the most important thing this technology will ever do. More than the chat products, more than coding help, as great as those are. So that's the metric I watch most closely.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes AI helping researchers find things faster as a useful collaborator from a more autonomous system that can run a meaningful part of a research program with a human mainly setting direction and checking the work.

fable-5.1.text:
I think we're closer than most people realize, but the shape of it is different from what we expected.

If you'd asked me a few years ago, I would have described "AI doing science" as a single threshold: one day the model can't, the next day it can. What's actually happened is much more gradual and much more uneven. The models are already extraordinarily good at some pieces of the scientific process. Literature synthesis, generating hypotheses, writing code to analyze data, catching errors in a derivation, suggesting an experiment someone hadn't considered. Researchers who use them well are noticeably faster, and we're starting to see results in math and some areas of biology and materials where the model contributed something that was genuinely not obvious to the humans in the loop.

What's still missing is the long arc. Real science is months or years of sustained judgment: deciding which problem matters, tolerating being wrong for a long time, knowing when a surprising result is a discovery versus a bug in your pipeline. The systems are getting better at longer-horizon tasks, and that's probably the single most important curve to watch. But I wouldn't say we have a model you can hand a vague open question to and walk away from for six months.

The other thing I'd flag is that the bottleneck is shifting. For a lot of fields it's no longer going to be ideas or analysis, it's going to be the physical world. Running the experiment, synthesizing the compound, getting time on the instrument. So part of what "autonomous science" requires is not just smarter models but better infrastructure around them, and a scientific culture that figures out how to verify and trust AI-generated results. I think that verification piece is where a lot of the hard work and the real safety questions are going to be.

My honest guess is that within a few years we'll have systems that can make small, real discoveries largely on their own, and that this will feel both less dramatic and more consequential than people imagine. Less dramatic because it'll happen one paper at a time. More consequential because that kind of compounding progress is, I think, the thing that actually changes the world.

r001.rationale: It describes current AI as helping researchers work faster on parts of the process, then distinguishes that from sustained autonomous science, which it says current systems cannot yet do independently for months.

astra-6.text:
I think the progress is exciting, but there’s still a big gap between helping a scientist and being able to do science on your own. A system can answer difficult questions or suggest an experiment, and that’s useful. But choosing the right question, running experiments, figuring out why your hypothesis was wrong, and staying with that process until you discover something new—that’s a much higher bar.

What I’d look for is a system that can make a discovery we didn’t know how to make, and that holds up when people independently test it. Then I’d want to see that happen repeatedly. We should judge this by the science that comes out, rather than how convincing the system sounds when it talks about science.

I expect we’ll see increasing amounts of meaningful work done by people and AI together along the way. That can be enormously valuable even before we have a fully autonomous scientist.

r001.rationale: It contrasts AI helping scientists—answering questions or suggesting experiments—with independently choosing questions, running experiments, testing hypotheses, and making discoveries.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we’ve made real progress, but there’s a big difference between a system that helps a scientist and one that can do science on its own. Models can be useful at connecting ideas, writing code, or suggesting hypotheses. The harder test is whether they can come up with an important question, design a good experiment, understand why it failed, and keep going until they discover something new.

What I’d look for is a system producing a result that surprises experts, that holds up when other people check it, and that wasn’t already implicit in the task someone handed it. And then doing that repeatedly. A compelling demo is one thing; a reliable process for discovery is another.

I’m optimistic, but I think we should measure progress by the quality of the science that comes out, rather than how much the system sounds like a scientist.

r001.rationale: It explicitly distinguishes systems that help scientists—by connecting ideas, writing code, or suggesting hypotheses—from systems that do science independently by framing questions, designing experiments, interpreting failures, and discovering results.
